stories.headline: S&P 500 AND NASDAQ HIT NEW ALL-TIME HIGHS AS OIL RETREATS ON HORMUZ CEASEFIRE
stories.body: S&P 500 rose 0.81% to a record 7,259 and Nasdaq gained 1.03% to 25,326 as WTI crude dropped 3.9% to $102.27 after the first tanker transited the Strait of Hormuz since Iran's closure. Easing supply-shock fears gave equities the green light — the Dow added 356 points to 49,298.

stories.headline: WTI DROPS 3.9% TO $102 AS FIRST TANKER CLEARS HORMUZ SINCE CLOSURE
stories.body: West Texas Intermediate settled at $102.27/bbl (-3.9%) and Brent fell 4% to $109.87 after a single tanker passage through the Strait of Hormuz signaled the ceasefire may be holding. Oil remains near 8-year highs but the 8-session rally appears to be cresting.

stories.headline: JOLTS: MARCH JOB OPENINGS HOLD AT 6.9M; HIRING SURGES 655K — NFP FRIDAY IN FOCUS
stories.body: Job openings held steady at 6.9M in March while hires jumped 655K to 5.6M, signaling a resilient labor market despite macro headwinds. Openings fell in professional services (-318K) but rose in finance (+98K). April NFP Friday — consensus 49K — is Warsh's first major data test as incoming Fed Chair.

stories.headline: MARCH TRADE DEFICIT WIDENS TO $60.3B; FACTORY ORDERS BEAT ON AI-LINKED ELECTRONICS
stories.body: The U.S. goods-and-services trade deficit expanded to $60.3B in March while factory orders beat expectations on strong AI infrastructure-linked electronics demand. The combination keeps import-driven inflation risk on the table even as oil eases.

stories.headline: PALANTIR BEATS EPS BY 5¢, FALLS 3%; PINTEREST POPS 15% ON Q2 REVENUE GUIDANCE
stories.body: Palantir posted Q1 adjusted EPS of 33¢ vs. 28¢ estimate but fell ~3% as investors weighed its stretched valuation. Pinterest jumped 15% after guiding Q2 revenue to $1.13B–$1.15B, topping the $1.11B consensus — ad-spend resilience is in focus heading into peak summer season.

stories.headline: MICHIGAN LANDS TOURNAMENT MOP CADEAU FOR 2026-27; ESTRELLA COMMITS FROM TENNESSEE
stories.body: Tournament Most Outstanding Player Elliot Cadeau commits to return to Michigan for 2026-27, while Tennessee big man J.P. Estrella transfers to Ann Arbor. The Wolverines are stacking talent around Dusty May's first national title core, immediately becoming a 2027 title contender.

stories.headline: PISTONS BEAT CAVALIERS 106-101 IN GAME 1; KNICKS CRUSH SIXERS 137-98 ON MONDAY
stories.body: Detroit took a 1-0 series lead over Cleveland in the Eastern Conference Semifinals, winning Game 1 106-101 at Little Caesars Arena. Monday, Jalen Brunson (35 pts) led the Knicks to a 137-98 demolition of the Sixers (61.4% shooting). In the West, Wembanyama set the all-time Playoff blocks record (12) but the Timberwolves edged San Antonio 104-102.

stories.headline: NFL SCHEDULE RELEASE TARGETING MAY 13; SEAHAWKS SIGN DE DANTE FOWLER
stories.body: The NFL is targeting Wednesday, May 13 for the 2026 schedule release featuring a record nine international games. Defending Super Bowl champion Seattle signed DE Dante Fowler to a 1-year deal worth up to $5M. Packers TE Tucker Kraft and Cowboys LB Micah Parsons are both expected back early in the season after ACL tears.

stories.headline: LANE KIFFIN TO LSU; TEXAS A&M OC COLIN KLEIN TAKES KANSAS STATE HEAD JOB
stories.body: Lane Kiffin departed Ole Miss to become LSU's head coach in the offseason's biggest coaching move. Texas A&M offensive coordinator Colin Klein takes the Kansas State head coaching job. With spring ball wrapped nationally, post-spring top 25 rankings have Oregon and Notre Dame near the top.

deepDive.title: What JOLTS Actually Tells Us About the Labor Market — and Why Hires Matter More Than Openings
content: Today's JOLTS report — job openings steady at 6.9M, hires surging 655K to 5.6M — got less attention than the oil move, but it's arguably more important for the Fed's June decision. As Kevin Warsh prepares to take the chair in mid-May, the labor side of the dual mandate is his most important constraint. Understanding what JOLTS measures, what it predicts, and why economists increasingly focus on hires rather than openings is essential context for interpreting Friday's April payrolls number.

The Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey captures a stock-and-flow picture of the labor market: the stock of unfilled positions (openings) and the monthly flow of workers moving into jobs (hires), out of jobs voluntarily (quits), and out involuntarily (layoffs). The Fed historically watched the openings-to-unemployed ratio as its preferred labor market tightness gauge — at its 2022 peak, there were 2.0 openings per unemployed worker, well above any prior cycle. That ratio has normalized to roughly 1.3x, signaling significant cooling. But today's data shows the hires rate spiked, suggesting businesses are converting existing postings into actual jobs — a healthier sign than a decline in openings driven by demand withdrawal.

The key academic insight, from Lazear and Spletzer (2012) and later Barnichon and Figura (2015), is that hires are a leading indicator of employment growth by 4–6 weeks, while openings are a lagging indicator of employer intent. When hires surge without a corresponding spike in openings, it suggests companies are filling positions faster — clearing inventory rather than posting new demand. That's what today's data shows: 655K more hires in March on roughly flat openings means the matching efficiency of the labor market improved sharply. For the Fed, this is a mildly inflationary signal — more employed workers = more wage income = more consumption — but not the wage-price spiral dynamic that would force an emergency hike.

For Warsh at the June 17 FOMC meeting, the read-through is nuanced. If Friday's April NFP confirms the 49K consensus, the labor market narrative becomes: 'job creation is slowing (fewer new payrolls) but the existing employed workforce is stable and active (high hires rate).' That's consistent with a soft landing rather than a hard one. The risk is the oil shock: if WTI stays above $100 through June, energy-driven CPI will run hot even as job growth softens — the stagflation combination that makes rate policy hardest. The hires surge gives Warsh one data point suggesting labor demand hasn't collapsed, which preserves his option to hold rather than cut in June — buying time to see whether the Hormuz situation fully resolves.
